items.title: Order of operations
items.content: Use brackets first, then powers, then multiplication/division left to right, then addition/subtraction left to right. BODMAS does not mean division always precedes multiplication.

items.title: Signs and operation properties
items.content: For multiplication/division, same signs give positive and unlike signs negative. Addition/subtraction follow number-line rules. Addition and multiplication are commutative; subtraction and division are not.

items.title: Fractions and decimals
items.content: Convert to common units or equivalent forms before combining. Division by a nonzero fraction means multiply by its reciprocal.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Rewrite ambiguous working with explicit brackets.
Check the sign and approximate size before accepting an answer.

items.title: BODMAS and nested brackets
items.content: Worked example: \(18-2[3+4]\div2=18-14\div2=18-7=11\). Brackets, then division, then subtraction.

items.title: Multiplication and division left to right
items.content: Worked example: \(24\div6\times2=4\times2=8\), not 2. Division and multiplication share priority.

items.title: Addition and subtraction with signs
items.content: Worked example: \(-7+12-5=5-5=0\). Moving right adds; subtracting moves left on the number line.

items.title: Multiplication and division signs
items.content: Worked example: \((-4)(-3)+(-12)/3=12-4=8\). Two negative factors produce a positive product.

items.title: Operation properties
items.content: Worked example: \(7(20+3)=7\cdot20+7\cdot3=161\). Commutativity permits \(3+7=7+3\), but \(7-3\ne3-7\).

items.title: Mixed fraction/decimal calculations
items.content: Worked example: \(1/2+0.25=0.50+0.25=0.75\). Choose exact fractions when they simplify the work.

items.title: Evaluate a numerical expression
items.content: Write one line per priority level and preserve brackets. Worked example: \(5+3\times(8-6)^2=5+3\times4=17\).

items.title: Handle chained multiplication/division
items.content: Proceed from left to right. Worked example: \(48/8\times3=6\times3=18\).

items.title: Estimate and check
items.content: Estimate the size and sign before exact work; substitute or use inverse operations to verify. Worked example: 198 × 51 is near 200 × 50 = 10,000; exact value 10,098 is plausible, and 10,098 ÷ 51 = 198.

items.title: Why multiplication distributes
items.content: Multiplication by a sum counts equal groups: \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\). This can simplify calculations without changing value.

items.title: Why left-to-right conventions matter
items.content: Multiplication and division have equal priority, as do addition and subtraction. A shared priority plus a fixed direction gives one unambiguous value.

items.title: Why dividing by a fraction uses its reciprocal
items.content: Multiplying by the reciprocal undoes multiplication by the divisor; the divisor must be nonzero.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Treating multiplication as always before division
items.content: They share priority; work left to right.

items.title: Dropping a negative sign
items.content: Use parentheses around negative numbers, especially when squaring or multiplying.

items.title: Changing the order of subtraction/division
items.content: These operations are not commutative.

items.title: Ignoring brackets
items.content: Resolve the innermost grouping first.

keyTakeaways: Brackets and powers come before multiplication/division.
Multiplication and division proceed left to right.
Subtraction and division are not commutative.
A negative times a negative is positive.
